title: Week 14 Mastery Quiz — Indigenous Americas and Oceania

questions.prompt: Which approach best compares Indigenous societies across the Americas and Oceania?
choices: Rank them by similarity to medieval Europe.
Treat all Indigenous societies as one civilization.
Compare specific societies, regions, periods, institutions, knowledge systems, and environments without assuming one universal path of development.
Use alphabetic writing as the main measure of complexity.
questions.explanation: Comparison should preserve historical specificity rather than impose a single external hierarchy.

questions.prompt: What does an engineered agricultural landscape such as chinampas or terraces most directly support?
choices: The environment automatically determined the political system.
All households had equal access to food.
The system remained unchanged for centuries.
Communities developed specialized ecological knowledge and coordinated labor; broader political conclusions require additional evidence.
questions.explanation: Environmental engineering supports claims about knowledge and coordination without proving deterministic political conclusions.

questions.prompt: Why is tribute alone insufficient evidence that a central state completely controlled subject communities?
choices: Obligation can coexist with local institutions, negotiation, resistance, uneven enforcement, and regional variation.
Tribute never existed.
Tribute documents cannot contain useful evidence.
Only archaeology can establish political authority.
questions.explanation: Political authority is relational and may vary across places and institutions.

questions.prompt: Which statement about quipu is methodologically strongest?
choices: Quipu should be dismissed because it is not alphabetic writing.

Quipu are Andean recording technologies whose meanings must be studied through surviving cords, context, comparison, and specialized scholarship without assuming they function exactly like alphabetic texts.
Every quipu has already been completely translated.
Quipu prove all Andean communities recorded identical information.
questions.explanation: Quipu require source-specific interpretation and should not be forced into alphabetic-writing categories.

questions.prompt: Which principle best guides study of societies without extensive surviving alphabetic archives?
choices: They have no recoverable history.
Rely exclusively on later colonial accounts.
Use archaeological, material, spatial, oral, visual, environmental, and other appropriate evidence and evaluate each source according to its own creation and transmission context.
Infer missing facts from modern stereotypes.
questions.explanation: Historical reconstruction can integrate multiple evidence traditions without privileging alphabetic archives automatically.

questions.prompt: Why should a European colonial account be corroborated when studying Indigenous societies?
choices: Because all written sources are false.
Because archaeology is always unbiased.
Because Indigenous sources never require contextualization.
Because outsiders wrote within particular languages, purposes, expectations, power relations, and encounter conditions that shaped what they observed and recorded.
questions.explanation: Colonial records can be useful, but provenance, encounter context, and independent evidence matter.

questions.prompt: Which description best treats Pacific wayfinding as a knowledge system?
choices: Navigation using accumulated observation and teaching involving stars, swells, winds, clouds, wildlife, seasonal patterns, memory, and other locally specific knowledge.
Random movement across the ocean.
A practice possible only after European instruments arrived.
One identical technique used by every Pacific community.
questions.explanation: Wayfinding integrates observation, memory, teaching, and environmental knowledge and varies across communities.

questions.prompt: What is the strongest interpretation of a map showing roads, settlements, or exchange connections?
choices: Every line proves direct political control.
The map can support spatial relationships and possible connectivity, while direction, frequency, volume, control, chronology, and causation require corroboration.
All mapped connections operated at the same time.
Distance has no effect on interpretation.
questions.explanation: Spatial evidence must be separated from unsupported causal or political inference.

questions.prompt: What is an appropriate rule when using living Indigenous knowledge in a school research project?
choices: Anything found online may be copied without attribution.
Treat community-held knowledge as public property.
Use appropriate public/authorized materials, preserve attribution and context, respect restrictions or community authority, and avoid presenting outsider interpretation as the community’s own voice.
Prefer anonymous summaries over Indigenous-authored sources.
questions.explanation: Ethical research respects provenance, attribution, context, community authority, and limits on access or representation.

questions.prompt: Which research design best answers how surviving evidence shapes histories of Indigenous societies?
choices: Use only the longest colonial narrative.
Choose evidence that confirms the initial thesis.
Treat all source categories as interchangeable.

Compare Indigenous/locally rooted sources appropriate for use, archaeology/material evidence, spatial/environmental evidence, and outsider records; identify corroboration, tension, destruction/survival bias, missing voices, and uncertainty.
questions.explanation: Multi-source corroboration reveals both historical patterns and the consequences of evidence survival and destruction.

shortResponse.prompt: Using at least three specific pieces of evidence from at least three source categories, explain how Indigenous societies in the Americas and/or Oceania developed complex systems of governance, knowledge, environmental adaptation, recordkeeping, or navigation. Then explain one limitation created by the evidence that survives.
shortResponse.exemplar: Full-credit work makes a specific defensible claim, avoids treating Indigenous societies as a single culture, uses accurate evidence from multiple source categories, explains rather than lists evidence, and identifies a meaningful evidentiary limitation, colonial-source problem, survival bias, or missing voice.
